newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn, opposition energy talks make little headway.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, opposition energy talks make little headway.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition made little headway in talks with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on controversial energy issues but agreed to meet again next Friday.

SPD party manager Franz Muentefering told reporters after the talks late on Thursday night that his party aimed to limit transports of nuclear waste across Germany, such as those that led to sometimes violent confrontations between police and demonstrators in Gorleben late last year.
The opposition also wants the government to begin work on nuclear waste storage in southern Germany, where many nuclear power plants are concentrated.

Gerhard Schroeder, who took part in the talks as premier of Lower Saxony where the Gorleben dump is located, and a leading potential SPD chancellor candidate in next year's elections, said an agreement on the waste issue could be reached in next week's talks.

But the SPD, which favours a phase-out of nuclear power, would not give its approval to a new generation of nuclear power reactors being jointly developed by German and French companies, Schroeder said in a radio interview.

The government side made clear there would be no further waste transports to Gorleben in the next two years, he said, adding that electric power industry executives, who were also invited to the talks, had accepted the idea that another dump in southern Germany was needed.

Environment Minister Angela Merkel and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, speaking for the administration, said transports would continue to be needed, as power plants have only limited capacity for medium-storage of waste.
Merkel said Germany must bring 110 Castor containers of waste back from processing plants in France by 2003.
Rexrodt added that the government hoped to clear the way for the new European Pressurised Reactor, being co-developed with France.
While Germany faces no immediate need for new nuclear power plants, the industry needs assurances that it will be possible to build such reactors in the future, Rexrodt said.
